examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/8797a50ddc0750a97190f96d8bc1cffe70c6ef9cc8e55a46f5a75d6b6702c81d.png)

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/347a44c388bd81e78d4dcf5f40584ce76273ffe25513ebb1522568ba479ac4fc.png) 
Describe the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $\mathbf{T}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf{T}$ is 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/94625329d7eba1da88a9dde36b6e64335a9801658a8c1fd054cea9db835ea4fa.png)

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-4\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $\mathbf{T}$ is non-invertible and the image of the triangle under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a line segment.

feedback.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=-2v-4,\,y=u+4v+6.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+y+a,\,v=bx+cy-2,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
feedback.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2v-4 \\ u+4v+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2v \\ u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 0-(-2)\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+4 \\ y-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (x+4)+1\cdot (y-6) \\ (-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (x+4)+0\cdot (y-6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x+y+2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}x-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+2,\,v=(-\frac{1}{2})x+0y-2.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+(-\frac{1}{2})+0=\frac{3}{2}.
$$
